INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

e option available, the method tends to be justified as the obtained mean directions could be interpreted in a meaningful way with respect to the mean early Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from Gondwanaland and the tectonic and thermo-chemical history of the region studied. The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Dual polarity observations were also made in Billy Creek equivalent beds on Kangaroo Island and in some sequences in the Amadeus Basin (Section III). In the latter basin, specimens from red beds in a

Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). Samples were taken either as separate sites generally consisting of 6-8 samples or, if conditions permitted, as stratigraphic profiles with each sample taken from a separate bed at regular 1-2 m intervals. Stratigraphic intervals were measured with a Jacob’s Staff and an attached Abney level. Mostly two specimens, 2.5 cm diameter and 2.25 cm height, were sliced from each core. Up to three specimens from each site, or one specimen from each third sample in case of stratigraphic profiles, have been subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization studies. The heatings were done in air in a furnace described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Because of the complexity of magne- tization, all pilot specimens were progressively demagnetized in 12-18 steps with decreasing temperature intervals up to 685°C. The intensity of suscep- tibility was measured after each heating step on a Digico bulk susceptibility unit. The remaining specimens were subjected to partial progressive demag- 258 netization in 8-12 steps over a selected temperature interval. Care was taken to keep the specimens in a very much reduced magnetic environment since the specimens tended to acquire Viscous Remanent Magnetization

components and failure to isolate separate components completely, further AFdemagnetization was not pursued for the bulk of the samples. All magnetic measurements were made on a SCT 2-axis super-conducting rock magnetometer which was interfaced to a Digico mini-computer for immediate data reduction. Directional analysis of all specimen components was made by means of orthogonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967, 1975). INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia INTRODUCTION Late Proterozoic and early Phanerozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Gondwanaland continents were reinterpreted recently by McElhinny et al. (19’7413) and McElhinny and Embleton (1976). Using selected pole positions, they showed that a common apparent polar wanderpath (APW) can be drawn when the main Gondwanaland fragments are reunited into the Smith and Hallam (1970) reconstruction. This common APW stretches from the ultimate Late Jurassic breakup backwards to at least 750 m.y. ago, thus implying unity of Gondwanaland during this period. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. One of the major uncertainties in constructing APW’s which span periods of appreciable polar movement is the inherent difficulty in assigning poles to either the normal or the reversed polarity group. Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia INTRODUCTION Late Proterozoic and early Phanerozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Gondwanaland continents were reinterpreted recently by McElhinny et al. (19’7413) and McElhinny and Embleton (1976). Using selected pole positions, they showed that a common apparent polar wanderpath (APW) can be drawn when the main Gondwanaland fragments are reunited into the Smith and Hallam (1970) reconstruction. This common APW stretches from the ultimate Late Jurassic breakup backwards to at least 750 m.y. ago, thus implying unity of Gondwanaland during this period. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

e option available, the method tends to be justified as the obtained mean directions could be interpreted in a meaningful way with respect to the mean early Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from Gondwanaland and the tectonic and thermo-chemical history of the region studied. The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Samples were taken either as separate sites generally consisting of 6-8 samples or, if conditions permitted, as stratigraphic profiles with each sample taken from a separate bed at regular 1-2 m intervals. Stratigraphic intervals were measured with a Jacob’s Staff and an attached Abney level. Mostly two specimens, 2.5 cm diameter and 2.25 cm height, were sliced from each core. Up to three specimens from each site, or one specimen from each third sample in case of stratigraphic profiles, have been subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization studies. The heatings were done in air in a furnace described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Because of the complexity of magne- tization, all pilot specimens were progressively demagnetized in 12-18 steps with decreasing temperature intervals up to 685°C. The intensity of suscep- tibility was measured after each heating step on a Digico bulk susceptibility unit. The remaining specimens were subjected to partial progressive demag- 258 netization in 8-12 steps over a selected temperature interval. Care was taken to keep the specimens in a very much reduced magnetic environment since the specimens tended to acquire Viscous Remanent Magnetization

INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

In fact, none of the Cretaceous samples showed reversed ma~etization and only one or two of them were reversely magnetized from each Triassic locality. The Mesozoic apparent polar wandering (APW) of the Transdanubian Central Moun- tains, determined from thermally isolated natural remanences at 13 localities, shows a remarkable similarity to the Mesozoic APW of Africa in that they both exhibit the same loop-like movement. Moreover, the difference between the two APW’s can practically be eliminated by a 35’ clockwise rotation of the palaeodeclinations. It is concluded, there- fore, that the region of the Transdanubian Central Mountains was part of the African (-Adriatic) plate up to some time in the Cenozoic when it moved to its present position, resulting in a 35O anticlockwise rotation relative to Africa. IDENTIFICATION OF MAGNETIZATION The magnetic properties of the fo~ations were discussed in the preceding section and it has been shown that magnetite is the chief contributor to the natural remanence. In the red limestones of lower Jurassic age haematite was also found to be an important remanence carrier and it was shown (M&-ton et al., 1980) that the directions of magnetization associated with magne- tite and haematite are parallel. Thus, we may conclude that the directions of the natural remanence represent the Earth’s magnetic field at the time of deposition or shortly after. It has also been shown that a high coercivity overprinting remanence of normal polarity associated with haematite pigment is present in the older Mesozoic formations. This secondary monetization is definitely pre- (upper) Tertiary because of its ch~a~teristic westerly declination and it is believed to be CRM acquired in late diagenetic processes during one of Mesozoic periods of normal polarity. In fact, this is the only characteristic remanence found in the Dachsteinkalk-limestone at Borzavh and in part of the crystalline lime- stone at Polgiirdi. The presence of this remanence rendered AF-demagnetiza- tion impracticable and it was only because its blocking temperature is lower

ause of its ch~a~teristic westerly declination and it is believed to be CRM acquired in late diagenetic processes during one of Mesozoic periods of normal polarity. In fact, this is the only characteristic remanence found in the Dachsteinkalk-limestone at Borzavh and in part of the crystalline lime- stone at Polgiirdi. The presence of this remanence rendered AF-demagnetiza- tion impracticable and it was only because its blocking temperature is lower than that of the primary remanence that the latter could be isolated by thermal demagnetization. CRM is not the only secondary magnetization encountered. It has been found that in purely magnetite-bearing rocks (e.g. the Tithonian limestone at Lokut-Hill) relatively high cleaning temperatures (400-500” C) were needed to destroy a secondary remanence which is attributed to VRM. Mountains, respectively. Figure 1 shows a simplified geologi- cal map (Dank and Fiiliip, 1967) with the sampling localities circles and numbered (cf. next section and Table I). The rocks collected are red, white and grey limestones and marls. 131 The magnetic measurements were done on a JR-4 spinner magnetometer with an rms noise level of 4 X 10 -6 Am-‘. All samples were thermally cleaned in a Schonstedt TSD-1 unit at temperatures determined from progressive demagnetization of pilot specimens. The relevant magnetic mineralogy was studied using remanent coercivity spectra derived from IRM aquisition char- acteristics (Dunlop, 1972). Magnetite and haematite were distinguished on the basis of their remanent coercivities, magnetite being the softer compo- nent, and the highest coercivity fraction was identified with pigmentary haematite. The thermal demagnetization characteristics and the remanent coercivity spectra together served as a means to infer whether the magnetiza- tion could be associated with the strati~aphic age of the rock. Polarities: Apart from the Jurassic limestone sections in which normal and reversed polarities occurred in about equal proportions, normal polarities prevailed both in the Triassic and Cretaceous collections. In fact, none of the Cretaceous samples showed reversed ma~etization and only one or two of them were reversely magnetized from each Triassic locality. The presence of the normal and reversed magnetizations may indicate NRM stability in general and so it is interpreted for Triassic and Jurassic sites. But the Cretaceous formations may all have been deposited during nor- mal polarity intervals including the Cretaceous normal period (Irving and Pullaiah, 1976) and with these just the lack of reversed polarity may be indicative of NRM stability. NRM directions: The tilt-corrected site mean directions are shown in Fig. 5 and we only point out here that they are reasonably precise and all are sig- nificantly different from the present field direction which is also valid for the uncorrected NRM directions. 137 Thus, the stability indicators also support the former conclusion that the thermally cleaned natural remanences are true records of the geomagnetic field at the time of sedimentation. Mesozoic palaeomagnetism of the Transdanubian Cen- tral Mountains and its tectonic implications. Tectonophysics, 72: 129-140. The Mesozoic apparent polar wandering (APW) of the Transdanubian Central Moun- tains, determined from thermally isolated natural remanences at 13 localities, shows a remarkable similarity to the Mesozoic APW of Africa in that they both exhibit the same loop-like movement. Moreover, the difference between the two APW’s can practically be eliminated by a 35’ clockwise rotation of the palaeodeclinations. It is concluded, there- fore, that the region of the Transdanubian Central Mountains was part of the African (-Adriatic) plate up to some time in the Cenozoic when it moved to its present position, resulting in a 35O anticlockwise rotation relative to Africa. Partial thermal demagnetization and thermomagnetic studies have been carried out on other sedimentary rocks, although the results did not consistently exhibit the extreme changes found here. There are some similarities between the results for the Sydney Basin rocks and those of Dunlop (1972). It is obvious that new minerals with a high susceptibility were formed during heating of the grey and drab silt- stones and sandstones. These results contrast with, for example, those of Shive and Diehl (1977) who reported work on red beds, and pointed out the importance of reduction of hematite to magnetite. It is possible that reduc- tion in the Sydney Basin rocks is caused by trace coal (Permian and Triassic) or detrital graphite (Triassic). Reduction promoted by vacuum pump oils is not a factor in this investigation. It is suggested that, apart from the reddened specimens, the magnetization in the sedimentary rocks in a DRM carried by detrital magnetite (perhaps hematized in part). Insofar as agreement was found between results from several rock types and differing magnetic techniques, there is good evidence to support the use of palaeomagnetic correlation. This hypothetical region existed between the Hida and the Mino terranes in the pre-early Mesozoic subduction period. The geologic ages of the rocks composing the Mino terrane range from the latest Paleozoic to middle Mesozoic, and the stratigraphic, tectonic, and sedimentologic relations among individual members are complicated owing to extensive internal deformation, as will be described in the next chapter. The Ryoke metamorphic belt, which is often regarded as the high-temperature counterpart to form the late Mesozoic metamorphic pair with the high-pressure Sambagawa metamorphic belt to the south, is a metamorphic derivative of the Mino terrane. Until some years ago, the Mino terrane was considered to be composed entirely of Paleozoic rocks deposited on a continental crust extended from the Precambrian Hida terrane (Fujimoto et al., 1962; Minato et al., 1965; Ada&i, 1976) (Fig. 1). INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: irections of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) have been determined, which are considered to be of pretectonic origin according to rock magnetic and structural geological evidence. A mean palaeopoie for the Devonian rocks in the areas investigated was determined at -29.7”N and 9.O”E. The site latitude derived from the Devonian rocks agrees very well with that observed in Great Britain and Britanny. The significant difference in longitude between our Devonian poles and the other European data may be due to an anticlockwise rotation of central Europe with respect to the northern Hercynian Foreland. The Carboniferous rocks yield a mean palaeopole at -41.7’N and 340.4’E. matching the Carboniferous part of the European polar wander path. A fold test within Carboniferous greywackes from the Hat-z mountains proves a pre-folding origin of the NRM of these rocks. However, this stable magnetization direction indicates local or regional tectonic displacement. Our results do not support any major latitudinal motions of continental segments in central Europe during the Hercynian orogeny. The Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Vosges, Franconian Forest, Harz, Britanny and Central Massif can be used to interpret the Hercynides in terms of a large scale shear belt. After appropriate cleaning characteristic directions of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) have been determined, which are considered to be of pretectonic origin according to rock magnetic and structural geological evidence. The site latitude derived from the Devonian rocks agrees very well with that observed in Great Britain and Britanny. The significant difference in longitude between our Devonian poles and the other European data may be due to an anticlockwise rotation of central Europe with respect to the northern Hercynian Foreland. GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Vosges In the Moldanubian part of the southern Vosges three sites were sampled 30 km north of Belfort in the Palaeozoic Markstein series. This lithological unit consists mainly of Upper Devonian and Lower Carboniferous greywackes and intercalated shales in marginal to basinal facies (R. Maas, pers. commun., 1981). In northern Slovenia (Yugoslavia, X = lSOE, ‘p = 46’N), 41 sites of Permo-Triassic red sandstones and volcanic rocks have been sampled for a palaeomagnetic study. The rock units are situated either in the Southern Alps or in the transition zone between the Southern Alps and the Dinarides. More than half of the sampled sites revealed that the primary remanence was seriously affected by partial or entire magnetic overprint in connection with the Alpine orogeny. This was manifested by either too steep inclinations, or too weak or inconsistent and unstable remanence. Only fourteen sites revealed the typical flat inclinations of Permo-Triassic rocks. INTRODUCTION Various reconstructions of the Western Mediterranean have been made in the recent years by combining geological and palaeomagnetic evidence (Dewey et al., 1973; Hsti, 1977; Channel1 et al., 1979; Vandenberg, 1979). A common feature was in all cases the assumption of an Adriatic microplate.

Previous studies (e.g., Louden, 1977) suggested that the nearby Philip- pine Sea plate drifted northward from the equatorial region and rotated clockwise by several tens of degrees. Plate movements of the subducting Pacific plate could have 21 produced additional displacements. Paleomagnetic work in several of the Bonin Islands was begun in 1980 in order to examine the validity of the tectonic movements suggested in previous models. Sampling was conducted on three Bonin Islands, namely Chichi-jima, Ani-jima and Ototo-jima. The paleomagnetic results from Chichi-jima, the geologically best known of the Bonin Islands are presented here together with the preliminary paleomagnetic data for the other Bonin Islands (Kodama, 1981). section_candidates.excerpt: BONIN ISLANDS The Bonin Islands consist of three groups of islands, each group lying about 50 km apart (Fig. 1). Each group is made up of a few islands and small islets up to some 20 km*. Since the end of the 19th century, the Bonin Islands have been studied by a number of scientists mainly from a petrological and paleontological point of view. Kikuchi (1890) first reported the characteristic pyroxene components in volcanic rocks on Chichi-jima. measurements were done with the help of a Schonstedt DSM-1A spinner magnetometer coupled with microcomputers (PDP-11 and APPLE II + ). Thermal cleanings were done in a non-magnetic oven (residual field = 8 nT) model TSD-I manufactured by Schonstedt Ltd. The apparent path wander of the poles obtained in the Vendee is compared with the one of stable Europe (western) and Gondwana: a convergence of the poles from the Vendee and stable Europe is observed from the beginning of Ordovician time and a reasonable similarity at Silurian time. This study partly fills the gap of palaeomagnetic data for the period: Upper Cambrian-Silurian for the Armorican plate. As early as Upper Cambrian, the Vendee was an integral part if the Armorican plate. Results of the first palaeomagnetic study carried out in the west Vendean region at the southern edge of the Armorican Massif are presented. The lithological units sampled range from Middle to Upper Cambrian and Silurian. After alternating field demagnetization and thermal cleaning, La Lombardiere basaltic rocks of Silurian age yielded only one residual component of magnetization (D = 214’, I = + 11’) after tilt correction. The corresponding palaeopole is located at 28’S, 321 “E. La Meilleraie sandstone and quartzite of Lower Ordovician age, which are equivalent to the Armorican sandstone, also contain one single residual component of magnetization (D = 244’, I = + So) after demagnetization and tilt correc- tion. The corresponding palaeopole is 15OS, 293OE. Finally, quart&es and rhyolites of Middle to Upper Cambrian age are characterized by two and possibly three components of magnetization. The mean direction of the main residual component after demagnetization and tilt correction is D = 319”, I = + 9”; the corresponding palaeopole position is 40°N, 222’E. cline. In his doctoral thesis (3rd cycle, unpublished), R. Wyns has shown that the Sigournais Formation lies stratigraphically above the Armorican sandstone and grades laterally into the Reaumur Group (Ordovician); however, the lack of a characteristic Ordovician fauna precludes a confirmation of this age relation. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) measurements were done with the help of a Schonstedt DSM-1A spinner magnetometer coupled with microcomputers (PDP-11 and APPLE II + ). Thermal cleanings were done in a non-magnetic oven (residual field = 8 nT) model TSD-I manufactured by Schonstedt Ltd. In the case of alternating field demagnetizations, either a GSD-1 Schonstedt apparatus (max. intensity = 100 mT) or a demagnetizer built at Lava1 University (Seguin, 1975) including a triaxial tumbler at three mu-metal concentric cylinders were used. This last apparatus can carry out demagnetizations up to 80 mT (peak-to-peak). All demagnetized NRM data were plotted on Zijderveld diagrams (Zijderveld, 1967) and where needed, various components of magnetization were isolated by vector subtrac- tion techniques. an zone sediments. During the past three years, the entire Early Jurassic to Late Eocene carbonate sequence from the Ionian zone has been sampled at 130 sites providing some 2500 samples. The suitability of these different rock types for palaeomagnetic research has been evaluated as part of a comprehensive palaeomagnetic investigation. This report summarizes the data from white and pink cherty micrites of Early Tertiary age from 51 sites in the Ionian Zone of northwestern Greece. These rock types are equivalent to the Scaglia limestones from Italy which have proved to give reliable palaeomagnetic directions in several investigations (Lowrie and Alvarez, 1975; Channel1 et al., 1978; Lowrie et al., 1982). TECTONIC SETTING OF THE IONIAN ZONE The pronounced similarities between the Jurassic sequences of the Ionian zone and of the Marche-Umbrian region of central Italy were first noted by Renz (1923). The Mesozoic sedimentary rocks from the Ionian zone closely resemble those of the Central Apennines and the Southern Alps and are comparable to the sediments flanking the western margin of the Central Atlantic (Bernoulli, 1967, 1972; Bernoulli and Jenkyns, 1974). The continuity of the South Tethyan carbonate facies from the Southern Apen- nines through the Dinarides and the H

initial identification of lithofacies and age the 1 : 50,000 Geological Maps of Greece were consulted. In the field where recent road cuts exposed fresh outcrops, distinctive lithological characteristics used by Greek geol- ogists served to differentiate between these two formations. In contrast to the uppermost part of the Vigla formation the upper part of the “Microbreccious Limestones” are characterized by chert lenses instead of chert bands, slightly thicker beds, more marly interbeds, and pronounced stylolites and laminations. To remove persistent uncertainty, all samples were routinely dated by micropalaeontological analysis of thin sections and washed samples. In addition, the Greek climate is conducive to the weathering of rocks. These factors combine to present the palaeomagnetist with a difficult task when searching for accessible outcrops fulfilling the above require- ments in the Ionian zone

Tectonophysics, 98: 1 l-27. On the basis of a pilot study of all the major carbonate lithologies in the Ionian zone of Western Greece., the upper part of the Upper Senonian to Upper Eocene “Microbreccious Limestones” formation was selected as the most suitable facies for a detailed regional palaeomagnetic study. The 51 sites sampled are situated on flanks of anticlines or monoclines which post-date the acquisition of the characteristic remanent magnetization. The regional folding occurred during post-Late Eocene emplacement of nappe sheets which had undergone decollement on Triassic evaporitic horizons. The palaeomagnetic directions after correction for deviations of local fold axis orientation have a regional significance. After this correction the mean palaeodeclination is about 35’E relative to the geographic pole. With respect to the Early T

98 1; Valente et al., 1982). During a study of the neotectonic features of the outer Aegean arc, Laj et al. (1982) collected Neogene samples from some of the Ionian and Aegean arc islands. They found evidence in sediments from Corfu of about 26” clockwise rotation with respect to the present geographic pole since the mid-Miocene. Data from Lower Oligocene to Upper Aquitanian Ionian flysch sections (Kissel et al., 1983) indicate a still earlier phase of some 30” additional clockwise rotation of Ionian zone sediments. During the past three years, the entire Early Jurassic to Late Eocene carbonate sequence from the Ionian zone has been sampled at 130 sites providing some 2500 samples. The suitability of these different rock types for palaeomagnetic research has been evaluated as part of a comprehensive palaeomagnetic investigation. This report summarizes the data from white and pink cherty micrites of Early Tertiary age from 51 sites in the Ionian Zone of northwestern Greece. These rock types are equivalent to the Scaglia limestones from Italy which have proved to give reliable palaeomagnetic directions in several investigations (Lowrie and Alvarez, 1975; Channel1 et al., 1978; Lowrie et al., 1982). The Cretaceous results show a post-Aptian/Albian counterclockwise rotation of about 25”, which is expressed by the smeared distribution of the Late Cretaceous site-mean results, and a post-Senonian (i.e. Tertiary) counterclockwise rotation of the same amount with respect to the pole. These results are in excellent agreement with contemporaneous paleomagnetic results from other peri-Adriatic regions. A Tertiary counterclockwise rotation of all the stable Adriatic block is strongly supported by the new results. ISCUSSION As pointed out before, the Gargano peninsula belongs to the stable Apulian platform which stretches below and all around the Adriatic Sea. In addition it is hardly deformed by the Alpine orogeny and therefore the paleomagnetic results from this stable platform are crucial for a correct interpretation of the geodynamics of the whole area including the Italian peninsula and western Yugoslavia. However, paleomagnetic results from this region recently gave rise to conflicting interpreta- tions. Channel1 (1977) argued that the paleomagnetic results point to a close relationship with the Southern Alps and that the Late Cretaceous paleopoles are not offset to the east relative to Africa by a post-Late Cretaceous counterclockwise rotation. VandenBerg and Wonders (1979) considered that Channel1 (1977) had given too much weight to the paleomagnetic data from Gargano by using site-mean results which had an a95 of more than or equal to 20’ for computation of the overall mean value. Actually VandenBerg and Wonders (1979) showed that if more severe reliability criteria are applied (CQ~ I 15’) the paleomagnetic data from southern Italy are not significantly different from those of northwestern Umbria, and hence led to a completely opposite interpretation (VandenBerg, 1979a, 197

agnetic results of northwestern Umbria (see review VandenBerg and Zijderveld, 1982). Recently Early and Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic data have become available from the Istria peninsula (Mkton and Veljovic, 1983). ISCUSSION As pointed out before, the Gargano peninsula belongs to the stable Apulian platform which stretches below and all around the Adriatic Sea. In addition it is hardly deformed by the Alpine orogeny and therefore the paleomagnetic results from this stable platform are crucial for a correct interpretation of the geodynamics of the whole area including the Italian peninsula and western Yugoslavia. However, paleomagnetic results from this region recently gave rise to conflicting interpreta- tions. Channel1 (1977) argued that the paleomagnetic results point to a close relationship with the Southern Alps and that the Late Cretaceous paleopoles are not offset to the east relative to Africa by a post-Late Cretaceous counterclockwise rotation. VandenBerg and Wonders (1979) considered that Channel1 (1977) had given too much weight to the paleomagnetic data from Gargano by using site-mean results which had an a95 of more than or equal to 20’ for computation of the overall mean value. Actually VandenBerg and Wonders (1979) showed that if more severe reliability criteria are applied (CQ~ I 15’) the paleomagnetic data from southern Italy are not significantly different from those of northwestern Umbria, and hence led to a completely opposite interpretation (VandenBerg, 1979a, 197

agnetic results of northwestern Umbria (see review VandenBerg and Zijderveld, 1982). The Upper and Lower Cretaceous limestones have an NRM carried by magnetite. Minor bedding tilt corrections improve the grouping of the site-mean results. The Upper Cretaceous “Scaglia” limestone (Turonian-Senonian) reveals a characteristic mean direction of decl. = 327.7”, incl. = 38.2O, a ss = 4.3’ (21 sites), while the Lower Cretaceous “Maiolica” limestone (Neocomian-Aptian/Albian) reveals a characteristic mean direction of decl. = 303.1 O, incl. = 35.1”. as,s = 8.7O (8 sites). The Cretaceous results show a post-Aptian/Albian counterclockwise rotation of about 25”, which is expressed by the smeared distribution of the Late Cretaceous site-mean results, and a post-Senonian (i.e. Tertiary) counterclockwise rotation of the same amount with respect to the pole. These results are in excellent agreement with contemporaneous paleomagnetic results from other peri-Adriatic regions. A Tertiary counterclockwise rotation of all the stable Adriatic block is strongly supported by the new results. Recently obtained palaeomagnetic data have given a fairly detailed apparent polar wander (A.P.W.) curve for the Mesozoic of the Transdanubian Central Mountains which has been compared with other A.P.W. curves from the Mediterranean area. The similarity of the A.P.W. curves enabled a unified A.P.W. curve to be constructed for the Central Mediterranean region. It has been shown that the new Mediterranean A.P.W. curve is in full agreement, even in details, with the updated A.P.W. curve for Africa. This confirms the existence during the entire Mesozoic of a single Central Mediterranean mega- tectonic unit rigidly attached to Africa. Its positions with respect to the pole can now be traced back

ithonian). The palaeomagnetic results summarized in Table I confirm the pole position for the Tithonian and permit us to construct a more refined apparent polar wander (A.P.W.) curve for the Mesozoic (Fig. 5). The A.P.W. curve exhibits the “African loop” as observed before (Mkton and MArton, 198 1) but this is more elongated now and has a hairpin bend at Late Jurassic-Early Cretaceous time. Recently obtained palaeomagnetic data have given a fairly detailed apparent polar wander (A.P.W.) curve for the Mesozoic of the Transdanubian Central Mountains which has been compared with other A.P.W. curves from the Mediterranean area. The similarity of the A.P.W. curves enabled a unified A.P.W. curve to be constructed for the Central Mediterranean region. It has been shown that the new Mediterranean A.P.W. curve is in full agreement, even in details, with the updated A.P.W. curve for Africa. It has been shown that the new Mediterranean A.P.W. curve is in full agreement, even in details, with the updated A.P.W. curve for Africa. This confirms the existence during the entire Mesozoic of a single Central Mediterranean mega- tectonic unit rigidly attached to Africa. Its positions with respect to the pole can now be traced back in more detail than before. Recently obtained palaeomagnetic data have given a fairly detailed apparent polar wander (A.P.W.) curve for the Mesozoic of the Transdanubian Central Mountains which has been compared with other A.P.W. curves from the Mediterranean area. The similarity of the A.P.W. curves enabled a unified A.P.W. curve to be constructed for the Central Mediterranean region. It has been shown that the new Mediterranean A.P.W. curve is in full agreement, even in details, with the updated A.P.W. curve for Africa. This confirms the existence during the entire Mesozoic of a single Central Mediterranean mega- tectonic unit rigidly attached to Africa. Recently obtained palaeomagnetic data have given a fairly detailed apparent polar wander (A.P.W.) curve for the Mesozoic of the Transdanubian Central Mountains which has been compared with other A.P.W. curves from the Mediterranean area. The similarity of the A.P.W. curves enabled a unified A.P.W. curve to be constructed for the Central Mediterranean region. It has been shown that the new Mediterranean A.P.W. curve is in full agreement, even in details, with the updated A.P.W. curve for Africa. This confirms the existence during the entire Mesozoic of a single Central Mediterranean mega- tectonic unit rigidly attached to Africa. Its positions with respect to the pole can now be traced back in more detail than before. IN

A palaeomagnetic study of the Helmsdale granite (U/Pb-420 m.y., K/Ar-400 m.y.), northeast Scotland, has revealed a multicomponent remanence dominated by two characteristic axes of magnetiza- tion. The suggested oldest of these magnetizations, the direction of which is nearly horizontal and directed N-S, is thought to have been acquired in Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian times. The existence of this shallow direction of magnetization discounts a recent hypothesis of a ea. 2000 km sinistral offset along the Great Glen Fault. The second component of ma~et~tion appears to be partly carried by haematite that apparently formed through disintegration of biotite and/or plagiociase. This secondary magnetization has a direction that can be associated with a Permian-early Mesozoic age. Similar overprinted magnetizations are characteristic features also in the Devonian sedimentary sequences north of Helmsdale. The present paper reports on the magnetic properties of the Helmsdale granite (Fig. 1) and discusses tectonic implications. The Helmsdale granite was emplaced into metasedimentary rocks of the Moine series. These results were rejected by Van der Voo and Scotese, but the interpretation of Storetvedt et al. gains support from the presented palaeomagnetic history of the Helmsdale granite as well from the results obtained for the lower Caithness Old Red Sandstone strata (Storetvedt and Torsvik, 1983, this volume). Figure 14 shows the Helmsdale poles in conjunction with relevant palaeomagnetic pole positions from western Europe. However, we question the reliability of these Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian results south of GGF, hence, they have not been included in Fig. 14. AF based data from the Arrochar and Garabal Hill-Glen Fyne igneous complex is unlikely to define single component directions owing to the pronounced elongated distribution of “cleaned” magnetic directions. For the same reason results from the Midland Valley have previously been questioned by Storetvedt (1970). The presented pole B from the Helmsdale granite is in better agreement with Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian results from Norway as well as with Devonian 127 results from Britain south of GGF. Re-examination of the Foyers granitic complex (a “newer” granite south of GGF; Rb/Sr 415 + 15 m.y., Hamilton et al., 1980) also yields a pole position in close agreement with the Norwegian result and does not differ significantly from the Helmsdale B pole (Torsvik, in prep.). Since our B pole represents a rock body situated to the north of the GGF, as opposed to the other results which are from south of the Fault (Fig. 14) it may be concluded that any movement along this fracture zone appears to be less than the

Alternatively, the relative polar wander path for Europe may follow a more westerly trend in Middle-Upper Devonian times (i.e. along the track marked by open arrows in Fig. 14 and not along the path indicated by solid arrows). It must be stressed, however, that in order to apply palaeomagnetic data to the displacement problem of the Great Glen Fault, it is vital to make the comparisons with rocks that have coinciding magnetic ages (which is not necessarily the physical rock age). Further detailed palaeomagnetic studies are therefore necessary. The A component has a pole position agreeing fairly well with a Permian-early Mesozoic palaeomagnetism for continental Europe. This age of magnetic overprint- ing is a characteristic feature of the remanent magnetization in the Devonian rocks north of Helmsdale. The A magnetization is probably related to hydrothermal alteration of the granitic body, associated with disintegration of biotite and/or plagioclase. This magnetization may be tied to the tectonic development (normal faulting) of the GGF, during which relative movement induced circulating meteoric water into the granite, causing the observed mineral disintegration and chemical precipitation (Tweedie, 1979). A palaeomagnetic study of the Helmsdale granite (U/Pb-420 m.y., K/Ar-400 m.y.), northeast Scotland, has revealed a multicomponent remanence dominated by two characteristic axes of magnetiza- tion. The suggested oldest of these magnetizations, the direction of which is nearly horizontal and directed N-S, is thought to have been acquired in Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian times. The existence of this shallow direction of magnetization discounts a recent hypothesis of a ea. 2000 km sinistral offset along the Great Glen Fault. The second component of ma~et~tion appears to be partly carried by haematite that apparently formed through disintegration of biotite and/or plagiociase. This secondary magnetization has a direction that can be associated with a Permian-early Mesozoic age. Similar overprinted magnetizations are characteristic features also in the Devonian sedimentary sequences north of Helmsdale. Re-examination of the Foyers granitic complex (a “newer” granite south of GGF; Rb/Sr 415 + 15 m.y., Hamilton et al., 1980) also yields a pole position in close agreement with the Norwegian result and does not differ significantly from the Helmsdale B pole (Torsvik, in prep.). Since our B pole represents a rock body situated to the north of the GGF, as opposed to the other results which are from south of the Fault (Fig. 14) it may be concluded that any movement along this fracture zone appears to be less than the

ccomplished by superim- posed normal and reverse B-axis components). Alternatively, the relative polar wander path for Europe may follow a more westerly trend in Middle-Upper Devonian times (i.e. along the track marked by open arrows in Fig. 14 and not along the path indicated by solid arrows). It must be stressed, however, that in order to apply palaeomagnetic data to the displacement problem of the Great Glen Fault, it is vital to make the comparisons with rocks that have coinciding magnetic ages (which is not necessarily the physical rock age). Further detailed palaeomagnetic studies are therefore necessary. The A component has a pole position agreeing fairly well with a Permian-early Mesozoic palaeomagnetism for continental Europe. This age of magnetic overprint- ing is a characteristic feature of the remanent magnetization in the Devonian rocks north of Helmsdale. The A magnetization is probably related to hydrothermal alteration of the granitic body, associated with disintegration of biotite and/or plagioclase. This magnetization may be tied to the tectonic development (normal faulting) of the GGF, during which relative movement induced circulating meteoric water into the granite, causing the observed mineral disintegration and chemical precipitation (Tweedie, 1979). The suggested oldest of these magnetizations, the direction of which is nearly horizontal and directed N-S, is thought to have been acquired in Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian times. The existence of this shallow direction of magnetization discounts a recent hypothesis of a ea. 2000 km sinistral offset along the Great Glen Fault. However, the available data are in favour of a few hundred kilometres sinistral movement along this fracture zone. However, the possibility of there having been a much larger transcurrent shift between Europe and North America in late/post-Devonian times, accumulated along various fracture zones within the Caledonian fold belt, is discussed. Clustering improved slightly for the combined data of the Malaguide locations (ESP I and ESP II). For the combined results of the Subbetic locations (SUB I, II & III), the F-test on the ratio of the concentration parameters is significant at a 95% level of significance (i.e. K/K* > FzcN_ ,)). The Subbetic data comprises normal and reversed paleomagnetic directions with typical low inclination values (Fig. 3). They depart significantly from the present local field direction. Together with the high blocking temperature (hematite) of the characteristic magnetization component, this justifies a comparison of the results with published data of Permo-Triassic age from Iberia and Africa. Despite the fact that the three Subbetic locations come from different tectonic units, the paleopole positions are broadly similar. Furthermore, the foldtest for the combined data shows a positive result. The results have therefore been combined and a mean paleopole has been calculated. SAMPLE PREPARATION AND MEASUREMENTS In the Paleomagnetic Laboratory of the State University of Utrecht (Fort Hoofddijk) core specimens (2.2 cm height, 2.5 cm diameter) were drilled from hand samples. Measurement of the natural remanent magnetization was carried out on the JR-3 spinner magnetometer and on the ScT cryogenic magnetometer. The specimens were subjected to stepwise AF-demagnetization to 300 mT and to thermal demagne- tization up to 700°C for separation of the various magnetization components. INTRODUCTION The geotectonic history of the Iberian peninsula as a continental block has been documented by paleomagnetic data which indicate a counterclockwise rotation of 35” relative to stable Europe. This rotation occurred between Barremian-Aptian and Maastrichtian time (VandenBerg, 1980). The relative position of the Internal Zone of the Betic Cordilleras-the alpine foldbelt of southern Spain-is, however, unknown for its entire history prior to the Miocene when it became attached to Iberia (Kampschuur and Rondeel, 1975). The Internal Zone consists of a number of nappe complexes that underwent considerable deformation prior to the deposition of Middle Miocene sediments (Rondeel and Simon, 1974). The metamorphic complexes comprise Nevado-Filabride * Present address: Koninklijke/Shell Exploratie & Produktie Laboratorium, Volmerlaan 6, 2288 CD Rijswijk, The Netherlands. 0040-1951/84/$03.00 0 1984 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 132 units, Alpujarride units and in addition in the eastern part, the Almagro and the Ballabona-Cucharon units. All of these complexes mainly contain sediments of Triassic and older age. The essentially non-metamorphic Malaguide Complex that tectonically overlies the Alpujarride Complex contains restricted amounts of younger

exes mainly contain sediments of Triassic and older age. The essentially non-metamorphic Malaguide Complex that tectonically overlies the Alpujarride Complex contains restricted amounts of younger rocks. The Internal Zone is in tectonic contact with the External Zone of the Betic Cordilleras (Fig. 1). The External Zone can be subdivided in a (par)autochthonous Prebetic realm in the north and an allochtonous Subbetic in the south. In the Miocene the Subbetic has been thrust, in northern direction, over parts of the Prebetic. The External Zone contains deformed Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous sediments which are considered to be deposited on the southern continental margin of the Iberian block (Hermes, 1978; Garcia-Hernandez et al.. 1980). INTRODUCTION The geotectonic history of the Iberian peninsula as a continental block has been documented by paleomagnetic data which indicate a counterclockwise rotation of 35” relative to stable Europe. This rotation occurred between Barremian-Aptian and Maastrichtian time (VandenBerg, 1980). The relative position of the Internal Zone of the Betic Cordilleras-the alpine foldbelt of southern Spain-is, however, unknown for its entire history prior to the Miocene when it became attached to Iberia (Kampschuur and Rondeel, 1975). The Internal Zone consists of a number of nappe complexes that underwent considerable deformation prior to the deposition of Middle Miocene sediments (Rondeel and Simon, 1974). The metamorphic complexes comprise Nevado-Filabride * Present address: Koninklijke/Shell Exploratie & Produktie Laboratorium, Volmerlaan 6, 2288 CD Rijswijk, The Netherlands. 0040-1951/84/$03.00 0 1984 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 132 units, Alpujarride units and in addition in the eastern part, the Almagro and the Ballabona-Cucharon units. All of these complexes mainly contain sediments of Triassic and older age. The essentially non-metamorphic Malaguide Complex that tectonically overlies the Alpujarride Complex contains restricted amounts of younger

exes mainly contain sediments of Triassic and older age. The essentially non-metamorphic Malaguide Complex that tectonically overlies the Alpujarride Complex contains restricted amounts of younger rocks. The Internal Zone is in tectonic contact with the External Zone of the Betic Cordilleras (Fig. 1). The External Zone can be subdivided in a (par)autochthonous Prebetic realm in the north and an allochtonous Subbetic in the south. In the Miocene the Subbetic has been thrust, in northern direction, over parts of the Prebetic. The External Zone contains deformed Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous sediments which are considered to be deposited on the southern continental margin of the Iberian block (Hermes, 1978; Garcia-Hernandez et al.. 1980). The,amphibolite suite was intruded between the Carn Chuinneag granite (ca. 560 Ma) and the late Caledonian pegmatites at ca. 450 Ma (Smith, 1979). The microdiorite-appinite suite cuts the 450 Ma pegmatites and predates the Strontian and Ross of Mull granites intruded at 420 Ma (Beckinsale and Obradovich, 1973; Smith, 1979). Thus the rocks of this study (excepting the lamprophyres) were uplifted and cooled with the regional metamorphic terrain and have a magnetic remanence record related, at least in part, to this post-tectonic late Caledonian event. Theoretical aspects of the acquisition of remanence during slow cooling have been treated by a number of workers (Ueno et al., 1975; Pullaiah et al., 1975; Dodson and McClelland Brown, 1980). The analysis of the latter workers shows that the magnetic blocking temperatures of rocks subject to the cooling rates of the Caledonides are only slightly lower than the unblocking temperatures determined in the laboratory implying that the uplift magnetisations are appreciably older than the K-Ar mineral ages.
