Thus the rocks of this study (excepting the lamprophyres) were uplifted and cooled with the regional metamorphic terrain and have a magnetic remanence record related, at least in part, to this post-tectonic late Caledonian event. Theoretical aspects of the acquisition of remanence during slow cooling have been treated by a number of workers (Ueno et al., 1975; Pullaiah et al., 1975; Dodson and McClelland Brown, 1980). The analysis of the latter workers shows that the magnetic blocking temperatures of rocks subject to the cooling rates of the Caledonides are only slightly lower than the unblocking temperatures determined in the laboratory implying that the uplift magnetisations are appreciably older than the K-Ar mineral ages. Some practical studies of uplift magnetisations in Precambrian rocks (Morgan 1976, Piper 1981) identify some of the main characteristics of remanence acquisition under conditions of slow cooling, namely the averaging of short term secular features of the magnetic field and the recording of time sequences of palaeopoles by higher to lower blocking temperature phases and earlier to later-cooled facies. Palaeomagnetism of Caledonian intrusive suites in the Northern Highlands of Scotland: constraints to tectonic movements within the Caledonian erogenic belt. Tectonophysics, 104: l-34. To evaluate the scale of tectonic movements within the northern sector of the 500-400 Ma Caledonian erogenic belt and its Precambrian foreland zone between the Great Glen Fault (GGF) zone to the southeast and the Laurentian Block to the northwest, we have studied the palaeomagnetism of minor intrusive rocks within the Northern Highlands terrain. These rocks include (1) amphibolites and other metamorphic rocks predating deformation, (2) microdiorities, dolerites and related suites emplaced, and probably magnetised, between 450 and 420 Ma, and (3) Lower-Middle Devonian lamprophyres. A range of predominantly NNE negative and SSW positive components are resolved by cleaning treatment with a dispersion of declinations towards a minority WNW-ESE axis; isolated southerly negative directed hematite-held components suggests limited, but no widespread, remagnetisation in Devonian-Carbonifer- ous times. Comparison is made with data from other tectonic divisions in the Caledonian erogenic belt and the bordering forelands. Palaeopoles from the Northern Highlands closely con

age and genetically linked to the younger granites; they cut most of these granites and occur as pebbles in the basal conglomerates of the Middle Old Red Sandstone sediments. The,amphibolite suite was intruded between the Carn Chuinneag granite (ca. 560 Ma) and the late Caledonian pegmatites at ca. 450 Ma (Smith, 1979). The microdiorite-appinite suite cuts the 450 Ma pegmatites and predates the Strontian and Ross of Mull granites intruded at 420 Ma (Beckinsale and Obradovich, 1973; Smith, 1979). Thus the rocks of this study (excepting the lamprophyres) were uplifted and cooled with the regional metamorphic terrain and have a magnetic remanence record related, at least in part, to this post-tectonic late Caledonian event. Theoretical aspects of the acquisition of remanence during slow cooling have been treated by a number of workers (Ueno et al., 1975; Pullaiah et al., 1975; Dodson and McClelland Brown, 1980). The analysis of the latter workers shows that the magnetic blocking temperatures of rocks subject to the cooling rates of the Caledonides are only slightly lower than the unblocking temperatures determined in the laboratory implying that the uplift magnetisations are appreciably older than the K-Ar mineral ages. age and genetically linked to the younger granites; they cut most of these granites and occur as pebbles in the basal conglomerates of the Middle Old Red Sandstone sediments. The,amphibolite suite was intruded between the Carn Chuinneag granite (ca. 560 Ma) and the late Caledonian pegmatites at ca. 450 Ma (Smith, 1979). The microdiorite-appinite suite cuts the 450 Ma pegmatites and predates the Strontian and Ross of Mull granites intruded at 420 Ma (Beckinsale and Obradovich, 1973; Smith, 1979). Thus the rocks of this study (excepting the lamprophyres) were uplifted and cooled with the regional metamorphic terrain and have a magnetic remanence record related, at least in part, to this post-tectonic late Caledonian event. GEOLOGIC SETTING Several hundred diabase dikes intrude the Piedmont province of South Carolina (Fig. 2). Many of them have not been mapped in detail and it is probable many more have yet to be mapped. A similar situation exists in Georgia and North Carolina where many early Mesozoic diabase dikes are known. Single K-Ar apparent ages of twelve diabase sites indicate that one half of the diabase dikes studied have ages near 195 m.y. Two of the sites, whose pole positions lie well to the east of our mean value, have apparent ages in the 180 m.y. range. Thus, while two groups appear to be present in South Carolina, it is the older group that seems to predominate. We combined our pole position with other data from diabase in the southern Piedmont (Watts, 1975; Bell et al., 1979) and have calculated a mean paleopole position of 86.1 “E, 66.4”N based on 50 sites in Georgia, South Carolina, and North Carolina. The southern diabase paleopole position plots slightly off the North American apparent polar wander path, but is not significantly different for the 190 m.y. average pole of Irving (1982). These results do not provide an indication of the degree of tilting of the Appalachians in post-early Mesozoic times. Since the 1979 survey, a portable spinner magnetometer (Chiron et al., 1981) has been used systematically to select sites with a minimum magnetization level, which has been fixed at 10F6 emu/cm, among those which are geologically significant. An electrical machine mounted on a frame and powered by a portable generator was used to drill the samples. The corer is a 25mm bronze barrel, 150 mm long, with a sintered diamond cutting edge. Water was sometimes used as a coolant but, as a routine, compressed air was used to cool the corer and to remove the dust, and this technique proved to be fast and lightweight. Orientation of cores was done with a special device. Even though the sediments have a very weak magnetism, a sun compass was used whenever possible, because it allows a more precise comparison between the directions of very distant sites (no corrections for regional magnetic anomalies are needed). The accuracy on orienta- tion is about 2”. A total of more than 2300 cores has been collected from 135 sites in the Aegean arc. The blue-grey colour itself is probably not the original colour of the sediments, but a result of chemical reduction phenomena due to their organic contents. Paleomagnetic measurements have been conducted on the M&Pliocene series along the external sedimentary Hellenic arc, in order td detect the presence or absence of rotational deformations in different sections of the arc. In the central-eastern part of the arc (Crete and Rhodes) paleomagnetic directions are very closely aligned along the North-South direction, showing that this portion of the arc has not undergone significant rotation since at least 7 m.y. (for Crete) and 4 m.y. (for Rhodes). In the western and northwestern parts, results from South Peloponnesos, Zakinthos, Kephallinia and Corfu indicate that this section of the arc has undergone a clockwise rotation. Detailed analysis of the data from the three Ionian islands shows that their rotation began about 5 m.y. B.P. and has proceeded since then at roughly 5

s direction in a zone of sinistral strike-slip faulting. These different motions have given rise to different underwater topographies in the two branches of the trench, which have been studied by seabeam and submarine surveys (Le Pichon et al., 1979a and b). The external arc along the trenches is subjected to compressional or strike-slip earthquakes whose slip vectors are directed roughly along the N48 direction in the west and along N22 in the east (Le Pichon et al., 1979a and b). The compressional zone of the external arc affects emerged lands only at the northwestern termination, in the Ionian Islands, where these compressional deformations (probably responsible for the present margin) began during the early Pliocene and were still active during the Pleistocene (Mercier et al., 1976). The great extent of these compressive struc- tures makes this region quite different from the rest of Aegea: indeed, the internal Aegean regions have been essentially submitted to a large scale extensional regime since the upper Miocene, and this regime has only occasionally been interrupted by compressive events, often quite moderate, in the upper Miocene-lower Pliocene and lower Pleistocene periods. Focal mechanism solutions show that the present regime is still extensional in all the

htly away from the external trenches, such as South Pelopon- nesos, Crete and Rhodes (McKenzie, 1972, 1978; Ritsema, 1973, 1974). In each of these regions, present-day stress directions, calculated from focal mechanisms or from in-situ measurements, are very close to the stress directions since the middle Pleistocene, as determined from the analysis of neotectonic faults and striations (Paquin et al., 1982, this volume). Thus, neotectonic analysis has allowed us to reconstruct the successive stress patterns in the Aegean arc since the upper Miocene. Using stress pattern analysis, different authors have considered the problem of the deformation of Aegea, and have suggested models for the geodynamical evolu- tion of the Aegean arc. Even if all the models come to the conclusion that the curvature of the arc has been acquired at least partially because of its tectonic evolution, the geodynamical mechanisms involved are substantially different accord- ing to the different authors. For instance Brunn (1976), Fig. 1, has suggested a model of continuous deforma- tion in which the curvature of the arc is related to the main Tertiary Alpine overthrustings, and was thus essentially completed before the neotectonic period. Paleomagnetic measurements have been conducted on the M&Pliocene series along the external sedimentary Hellenic arc, in order td detect the presence or absence of rotational deformations in different sections of the arc. In the central-eastern part of the arc (Crete and Rhodes) paleomagnetic directions are very closely aligned along the North-South direction, showing that this portion of the arc has not undergone significant rotation since at least 7 m.y. (for Crete) and 4 m.y. (for Rhodes). In the western and northwestern parts, results from South Peloponnesos, Zakinthos, Kephallinia and Corfu indicate that this section of the arc has undergone a clockwise rotation. Detailed analysis of the data from the three Ionian islands shows that their rotation began about 5 m.y. B.P. and has proceeded since then at roughly 5

s direction in a zone of sinistral strike-slip faulting. These different motions have given rise to different underwater topographies in the two branches of the trench, which have been studied by seabeam and submarine surveys (Le Pichon et al., 1979a and b). The external arc along the trenches is subjected to compressional or strike-slip earthquakes whose slip vectors are directed roughly along the N48 direction in the west and along N22 in the east (Le Pichon et al., 1979a and b). The compressional zone of the external arc affects emerged lands only at the northwestern termination, in the Ionian Islands, where these compressional deformations (probably responsible for the present margin) began during the early Pliocene and were still active during the Pleistocene (Mercier et al., 1976). The great extent of these compressive struc- tures makes this region quite different from the rest of Aegea: indeed, the internal Aegean regions have been essentially submitted to a large scale extensional regime since the upper Miocene, and this regime has only occasionally been interrupted by compressive events, often quite moderate, in the upper Miocene-lower Pliocene and lower Pleistocene periods. Focal mechanism solutions show that the present regime is still extensional in all the

htly away from the external trenches, such as South Pelopon- nesos, Crete and Rhodes (McKenzie, 1972, 1978; Ritsema, 1973, 1974). In each of these regions, present-day stress directions, calculated from focal mechanisms or from in-situ measurements, are very close to the stress directions since the middle Pleistocene, as determined from the analysis of neotectonic faults and striations (Paquin et al., 1982, this volume). Thus, neotectonic analysis has allowed us to reconstruct the successive stress patterns in the Aegean arc since the upper Miocene. Using stress pattern analysis, different authors have considered the problem of the deformation of Aegea, and have suggested models for the geodynamical evolu- tion of the Aegean arc. Even if all the models come to the conclusion that the curvature of the arc has been acquired at least partially because of its tectonic evolution, the geodynamical mechanisms involved are substantially different accord- ing to the different authors. For instance Brunn (1976), Fig. 1, has suggested a model of continuous deforma- tion in which the curvature of the arc is related to the main Tertiary Alpine overthrustings, and was thus essentially completed before the neotectonic period. More recently (Lybbris et al., 1980, 1981) the discovery of longitudinal variations of deformation in the Kithiran strait as shown by seabeam bathymetric studies and by the existence of en echelon faults, has led these authors to modify their original model. Thus, in the model presented at this conference, Crete is “decoupled” from Peloponnesos and does not show any appreciable rotation. All these models are based on seismic and tectonic data. An important parameter which cannot be attained by these methods is the rotational deformation and its variations along the arc. The initially north-south magneti- zation of the sediments can, in principle, provide a primitive and constant geometri- cal element along the arc; its deviations with respect to the initial direction in different regions can provide data about the rotational deformations of the arc. Their location is shown on the schematic map in Fig. 2. All the sampled regions have been submitted to quatemary uplift movements which have caused out~ropp~g of large parts of Neogene sedimentary basins. Most of the deposits are of marine origin and thus a stratigraphical age can often be assigned to them, u

an arc. The sedimen- tary evolution of these basins has been described in numerous previous works (Drooger and Meulenkamp, 1973; Fortuin, 1978; Guernet, 1978; Angelier, 1979). Essentially, these basins have been submitted to extensional tectonics, sometimes with huge normal faults, during both the sedimentation and the emersion periods. This tectonics was very active since at least the Serravallian (13 m.y.) in Crete (Angelier, 1979) and continued during the deposition of the lacustrine levantine series in Rhodes (Gauthier, 1979) where the deposits are attributed to the upper Fig. 2. Thus, in the model presented at this conference, Crete is “decoupled” from Peloponnesos and does not show any appreciable rotation. All these models are based on seismic and tectonic data. An important parameter which cannot be attained by these methods is the rotational deformation and its variations along the arc. Recent progress in both the technology and understanding of the pal~magnetism of sedimentary rocks now allows the use of their weak remanent magnetization for geological purposes. An electrical machine mounted on a frame and powered by a portable generator was used to drill the samples. The corer is a 25mm bronze barrel, 150 mm long, with a sintered diamond cutting edge. Water was sometimes used as a coolant but, as a routine, compressed air was used to cool the corer and to remove the dust, and this technique proved to be fast and lightweight. ies. The extent of these internal defo~ations has led Mercier (1977) and Mercier et al. (1976, 1979) to the notion of the continuum of deformation. In their opinion, the Aegean domain constitutes the plastically deformed edge of the Euro-Asiatic plate. The prolongation of the northern Anatolian strike-slip faults into the northwestern Aegean Sea and the discovery of faults with a sinistral strike-slip component in Macedonia have led Mercier et al. (1979) to consider that the defo~ation of this region of northern Aegea may be described by a scheme of slip lines, as suggested by Tapponnier. This evolutionary scheme implies rotational deformations of the Aegean lithosphere, clockwise in the northwest and anticlockwise in the southeast of the arc, Le Pichon and Angelier (1979) consider the neotectonic movement since 13 m.y. to be a first appro~mation of the clockwise rotation of a rigid plate by approx. 30” about an eulerian pole, located near 4WN, 18’E in the southern Adriatic Sea. f a rigid plate by approx. 30” about an eulerian pole, located near 4WN, 18’E in the southern Adriatic Sea. An important back arc distension, indicated by intensive normal faulting in the Aegean Sea, is superimposed upon this rigid rotation and modifies its value locally all along the external arc: there is thus maximum rotation in the northwest (Ionian Islands except Corfu) decreasing towards the southeast to attain zero near eastern Crete. According to them, western Crete appears to undergo a clockwise rotation, causing a torsion of the island. More recently (Lybbris et al., 1980, 1981) the discovery of longitudinal variations of deformation in the Kithiran strait as shown by seabeam bathymetric studies and by the existence of en echelon faults, has led these authors to modify their original model. Thus, in the model presented at this conference, Crete is “decoupled” from Peloponnesos and does not show any appreciable rotation. All these models are based on seismic and tectonic data. An important parameter which cannot be attained by these methods is the rotational deformation and its variations along the arc. An electrical machine mounted on a frame and powered by a portable generator was used to drill the samples. The corer is a 25mm bronze barrel, 150 mm long, with a sintered diamond cutting edge. Water was sometimes used as a coolant but, as a routine, compressed air was used to cool the corer and to remove the dust, and this technique proved to be fast and lightweight. Orientation of cores was done with a special device. Paleomagnetic measurements have been conducted on the M&Pliocene series along the external sedimentary Hellenic arc, in order td detect the presence or absence of rotational deformations in different sections of the arc. In the central-eastern part of the arc (Crete and Rhodes) paleomagnetic directions are very closely aligned along the North-South direction, showing that this portion of the arc has not undergone significant rotation since at least 7 m.y. (for Crete) and 4 m.y. (for Rhodes). In the western and northwestern parts, results from South Peloponnesos, Zakinthos, Kephallinia and Corfu indicate that this section of the arc has undergone a clockwise rotation. Detailed analysis of the data from the three Ionian islands shows that their rotation began about 5 m.y. B.P. and has proceeded since then at roughly 5

f a rigid plate by approx. 30” about an eulerian pole, located near 4WN, 18’E in the southern Adriatic Sea. An important back arc distension, indicated by intensive normal faulting in the Aegean Sea, is superimposed upon this rigid rotation and modifies its value locally all along the external arc: there is thus maximum rotation in the northwest (Ionian Islands except Corfu) decreasing towards the southeast to attain zero near eastern Crete. According to them, western Crete appears to undergo a clockwise rotation, causing a torsion of the island. A paleomagnetic study of Late Mesozoic dolerite dykes and sills and Paleozoic sediments from Spitsbergen, the main island of the Svalbard Archipelago, gives the position of the pole in the Late Mesozoic and Paleozoic as distinct from the corresponding poles of Europe and North America. The Paleozoic pole is to the south of corresponding poles for Europe and North America. The data suggest that Svalbard has moved independently of Europe and North America at least in the Late Mesozoic, and thus might behave as a microplate or block. Sampled rocks consist mainly of marly limestones, arenaceous limestones and cherty limestones (Siedlecka, 1970). All rocks are highly carbonaceous. Deposition of limestones under study occurred in uniform conditions, in a warm, arid climate, in a marine environment with eustatic changes of sea level (Birkenmajer, 1964). The magnetic mineralogy of limestones is difficult to describe optically because of the small grain size and the low concentration. According to Lowrie and Heller (1982) magnetic techniques are more promising. In the case of Spitsbergen limestones, extraction and concentration of the magnetic minerals failed. The only method is to observe the decay of saturation remanence Z,, during continuous heating in a field-free space. There have been no serious tectonic events in Spitsbergen since the Devonian (Harland, 1969; Birkenmajer, 1981 j which might be responsible for widespread remagnetization of the Paleozoic limestones. The overprint of Mesozoic igneous events has been recognized and isolated. The geomagnetic field obtained for the Paleozoic sediments from Spitsbergen has normal polarity. In the period between the Late Carboniferous and Late Permian the geomagnetic field had predominantly reverse polarity. A paleomagnetic study of Late Mesozoic dolerite dykes and sills and Paleozoic sediments from Spitsbergen, the main island of the Svalbard Archipelago, gives the position of the pole in the Late Mesozoic and Paleozoic as distinct from the corresponding poles of Europe and North America. The Paleozoic pole is to the south of corresponding poles for Europe and North America. The data suggest that Svalbard has moved independently of Europe and North America at least in the Late Mesozoic, and thus might behave as a microplate or block. It would have been provoked by substantial invasions of fluids percolating through the carapace of volcanic material. An important fracturing appears to have controlled the distribu- tion of the effects of this metamorphism. The temperature conditions remained relatively low, certainly below 400°C. The mobilisation of elements such as Ca, Fe, Na, K, and sometimes Si, was widely facilitated. Only the end of this phenomenon is clearly marked by the important phase of plutonic activity radiochronologically dated to the Miocene and whose products are exempt from all transformation. This metamorphism is obviously an element of primary importance for the interpretation of geochronological and palaeomagnetic data. Neogene rocks are exempt from this metamorphism. The metamorphic episode would thus be situated at the Oligocene-Miocene boundary. Most of these formations have been moved to a greater or lesser degree, either because of major folding in neighbouring regions, or as a result of a widely developed tectonic breaking.
